claude.result:
ASHFALL OUTPOST is complete at `./game.html` (~2050 lines, single self-contained file, no external resources, no browser storage, no `Math.random`).

Implemented in full: seeded mulberry32 core loop with a fixed documented turn-resolution order; an 8×8 procedurally-generated map (ash flat/rock/water/vent/ruins) with terrain-gated buildings and adjacency bonuses; a real two-stage production chain (ore→metal, ash→soil→food) with storage caps and logged overflow; individual colonists with 4 fixed jobs, skill growth, fatigue, and morale that drives output and can cause colonists to leave; a 10-node research tree with prerequisites; 14 weighted events with cooldowns (5 offering genuine 2–3-way tradeoffs); a caravan trade system with scarcity/drift-based pricing; ashstorms that scale with turn count and damage buildings until repaired; JSON save/load with validation (no browser storage); win/lose/time's-up conditions with a scored summary screen; a full tabbed UI with hover/tap tooltips, non-color status indicators, and keyboard shortcuts (Space, 1-5); and a Dev panel with 32 invariant assertions and a headless 200-turn deterministic benchmark (with a one-click "run twice, verify identical hash" button).

Since I couldn't execute JS in this sandbox to test it live, I compensated with a rigorous static review: confirmed brace/paren/tag balance across the whole file, traced every HTML id against its JS/CSS references, and read through the entire script section by section. That caught and fixed three real bugs before delivery — a missing `</script></body>` (the original edit had dropped it), map-legend swatches all rendering the same grey due to a CSS specificity mismatch, and the log panel's scroll styling silently never applying because its selector referenced a nonexistent `#logpanel` id (plus a resulting ordering fix) — and one interaction bug where Space would double-fire when a tile or button had focus.

Given I couldn't launch a browser here, you'll want to open the file yourself to confirm it plays as expected — I'd treat this as reviewed-but-not-hands-on-tested.
